## 3.1 If-else branches (general)

A branch is a sequence of statements only executed under a certain condition.

Don't compare floating point numbers :)

String comparisons aren't simple == or other operations. It won't work if you do something like myString == "Hello". It will compile but it will cause a logic error

When using range comparisons, remember to always go from small to big otherwise a logic error is going to make a branch execute when you don't want it to

## 3.9 Order of evaluation

The order in which operators are evaluated in an expression are known as precedence rules.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Bitwise operators perform AND or OR on corresponding individual bits of the operand. They are highly-specialized and not common in beginning programs and not discussed here.

It's using & or | instead of && or ||

A common error is to use a bitwise operator instead of a logical operator. It may yield different behavior than expected.
#OrderOfEvaluation 

## 3.11 Switch statements

A switch statement can more clearly represent multi-branch behavior involving a variable being compared to constant values. The program executes the first case whose constant expression matches the value of the switched expression, executes that case's statements, and then jumps to the end. If no case matches, then the default case statements are executed.

The statement's expression should be an integer, char, or string. It should not be Boolean or a floating-point type. Each case must have a constant expression, no variables. (dunno if it means finals tho). Usually put in numerical order with the default at the end. Always include a default unless there's a specific reason.

NOTE: Omitting the break statement for a case will cause the statements within the next case to be executed. It can sometimes be useful. The execution falls through to the next switch case even if the expressions do not evaluate to true.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

## 3.13

You can compare strings using the annotation str1.equals(str2). It returns true if the two strings are the same length and each character is identical (case matters).

Using == only compares memory addresses

Strings can be compared relationally (less than, greater than), as when sorting words alphabetically. It begins at index 0 and compares each character until the evaluation results in false or the end of a string is reached.

It compares the ASCII table numbers.

If strings are identical to a point and then one is longer than the other, the longer one is greater than

![](data:image/png;base64,)

You can compare strings while ignoring case using `str1.equalsIgnoreCase(str2)` and `str1.compareToIgnoreCase(str2)`

## 3.17: Conditional expressions

![](data:image/png;base64,)

A conditional expression has the form condition ? exprWhenTrue : exprWhenFalse. For example:

(x == 2) ? 5 : 9 * x

if x is 2 then it evaluates to 2

Conditional expressions have three operands and thus the "?" and ":" together are sometimes referred to as a ternary operator.
#ConditionalExpression

## 3.18: Floating-point comparison

You shouldn't use equals when comparing floating points. Floating point math isn't precise and when it is, it is often not the exact value the programmer is looking for. Like if the expression is floatPoint == 0.7, theres a good chance it's actually 0.699999999999995559etc, which would evaluate to false.

Instead, compare floats for 'close enough'.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

The difference threshold indicating that floating-point numbers are equal is often called the epsilon. Epsilon's value depends on the program's expected values, but 0.0001 is common.
